title: Students vs. Scholars
author: George Cusack
summary: George Cusack, a professor at Carleton University, reframes first-year students as 'scholars' from day one -- active knowledge contributors rather than passive knowledge recipients. He argues that students locked in a purely transactional mentality focus exclusively on grade optimization, avoiding genuine intellectual risk-taking and the curiosity that productive academic work requires. This transactional framing also distorts how students engage with AI: they treat it as a grade-efficiency tool rather than as an object of critical inquiry. Students who adopt a scholar identity become curious about AI's capabilities and limitations, willing to share discoveries with peers, and more capable of evaluating AI as scholars rather than as consumers. Cusack offers a concrete assignment -- having student-scholars test AI capabilities and report findings -- as a practical entry point for building genuine AI literacy in any discipline.
points: * A 'student' receives knowledge passively; a 'scholar' actively seeks to add something new -- Cusack places this distinction at the front of every syllabus. * The transactional mentality steers students toward the path of least resistance: familiar concepts, avoided risk, and work that no one genuinely cares about. * Students in transactional mode approach AI strategically (avoiding honor code risks, cutting workload), whereas scholar-identified students approach AI with curiosity about its limits. * Creating classroom space for sharing AI experiments builds a genuine community of inquiry and shifts how students relate to both research and technology. * The scholar reframe shifts academic work from grade extraction to genuine contribution to a shared knowledge community.
quotes: From this moment onward, you're not just a student; you're also a scholar.
A student's job is to receive knowledge. Being a student is a largely passive occupation, as students aren't usually expected to contribute anything new to the ideas or conversations they encounter.
A scholar, by contrast, seeks out knowledge with the specific goal of adding something new to what is known or understood on a given subject.
The purely transactional approach completely precludes curiosity as an asset to academic work.
If students see themselves as passive recipients of knowledge, then they will learn to use AI in ways that reinforce that passivity.
When students adopt the mentality of scholars, though, they're more willing to see AI as a site of curiosity.
By creating that space, you open the possibility for you and your student-scholars to develop your understanding of AI together, which is the way a community of scholars should work.
